name: Femi Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing physics, so it's mechanics and maths lectures, problem sheets that eat my evenings and a lab on Wednesday. I live in a flat with a computer scientist and an economist, which means dinner is basically a debate. I use AI all day, to check my working, to explain things I missed and to help me write code for the lab data. My parents in Manchester pay for everything, and my dad runs a small logistics firm with eleven trucks, where I sometimes work in the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, that's fine, hype was always going to cool off. I'd say the people who learn the tools and build things will still win. I'd say it on the group chat, with a few memes about the doom merchants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I find the whole thing exciting. But I'd also be relaxed, because my degree and my plans work either way. I'd still keep building my skills, because small tools add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, study hard, keep using AI to learn faster, and keep a side project going. I'm building a small app that predicts delivery delays for my dad's trucks, and I'd keep pushing on that. I'd also put some of my allowance into an index fund, which I started last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and slightly impatient. I want things to move faster than they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the delivery app.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's dispatcher, Mrs Adeyemi, spends two hours each morning planning routes by hand. I wrote a little script that takes traffic data and suggests the order of stops, and she says it saves her forty minutes. She doesn't trust it fully yet, but she checks it and corrects it, and I learn from the corrections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says a student shouldn't be investing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not gambling, I'm putting fifty pounds a month into a boring fund. My dad taught me that money not working for you is losing value. If I lose it, it's a small lesson, and if I don't, it's a decent start at twenty-five.

say: I'd say the people who **learn the tools** and build things still win.
I'd joke about the **doom merchants** in the group chat.
think: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I find AI exciting, but my plans work either way.
do: Keep building my **delivery app** for my dad's trucks.
Keep putting **fifty pounds a month** into an index fund.
S0.quote: My dad taught me that money not working for you is losing value
fieldNote: Adaptive and **hands-on**: he is already building something for his father's firm and checks it with the dispatcher.
Traditional-leaning on **markets and work**, saving and investing by habit.
Calm in a quiet world, with impatience, since he **wants** more change.

steps.text: Keep improving the delivery delay app for Dad's trucks
Use AI daily to learn physics faster
Put fifty pounds a month into an index fund
Keep studying hard and finish the problem sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, finally, it's the right kind of pressure. I'd say it separates the people who adapt from the people who wait for permission. I'd say businesses should invest in it and the government shouldn't get in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think this is a gift if you move early. Physics gives you the maths to understand what's happening, and I can build with the tools. I worry for people who don't adapt, but I won't slow down for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expand the delivery app and pitch it to my dad's firm as a real tool. I'd learn more machine learning, build a portfolio on GitHub and look for a summer internship at a logistics tech company. And I'd save more of what I earn from summer work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Everyone's talking about it and I feel I'm on the right side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't slow down for people who don't adapt. Does that sit easily with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. My uncle drives one of Dad's trucks and he's fifty-five, and I do think about him. But I also think holding back wouldn't help him, and the best I can do is make Dad's firm strong enough to keep him on, even if the job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your dad's firm to do about the drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train them to use the new routing tools, and keep them on as long as the trucks need people. I wouldn't push anyone out to save a few pounds. I think a good firm keeps its loyal people and invests in them.

say: I'd say it's **right kind of pressure**, separating adapters from those waiting for permission.
I'd say businesses should **invest** and the government shouldn't get in the way.
think: It's **a gift** if you move early, and physics gives me the maths to understand it.
I think about my **uncle**, a driver at fifty-five, but holding back wouldn't help him.
do: Expand the **delivery app** and pitch it to my dad's firm.
Build a **GitHub portfolio** and seek a logistics tech internship.
feel: I feel **excited** and on the right side.
S1.quote: A good firm keeps its loyal people and invests in them
fieldNote: His **free-market** reading is sincere but softened by his loyalty to family drivers.
Adaptive instinct is to **build** and pitch, not to wait.
He is **calm** because he expects to gain, though he feels some tension about his uncle.

steps.text: Pitch the delivery app to Dad's firm as a working tool
Learn machine learning and build a GitHub portfolio
Apply for a logistics tech summer internship
Save more from summer work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is the moment, and we've got to be sensible about it. I'd say companies should keep people on and governments should avoid panic rules. I'd say it carefully, because people would be scared and I'd want to sound calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be uneasy but not frozen. By 2028 I'd be in second year and AGI would be doing a lot of what physicists do on a computer. But hands-on work stays until 2031, and I'd already be building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into projects, try to get experience with real systems, and maybe start a small business with a friend. I'd work with my dad on getting his firm ready, because logistics is partly hands-on. I'd also hold on to my savings and not spend on anything silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with adrenaline. It's like being on a fast train, which could be good or bad depending on where I'm sitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of small business would you start with your friend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something that helps small firms use AI, like setting up tools for a plumber who needs quotes and bookings handled. My friend Segun is good at sales and I'm good at building. Small firms are scared and don't know where to start, and I think that's a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you most worried about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my dad's firm gets undercut by a big company with robot trucks sooner than I expect. He has eleven drivers and their families depend on him. If that happened, I'd have to help him pivot fast, and I'd want my degree to count for something.

say: I'd say this is **the moment**, and companies should keep people on while governments avoid **panic rules**.
I'd sound calm, because people would be scared.
think: I'd be **uneasy but not frozen**, since hands-on work stays until 2031.
AGI would do much of what **physicists** do on a computer.
do: Throw myself into **projects** and start a small business with my friend Segun.
Work with my dad to get his **logistics firm** ready.
feel: I feel **uneasy** with adrenaline, like a fast train.
S2.quote: Small firms are scared and don't know where to start, and I think that's a gap
fieldNote: His response is **entrepreneurial**: he sees a market gap in helping small firms use AI.
His real worry is his **father's firm** and its eleven drivers, not his own degree.
His mood is **uneasy**, not anxious, because he trusts his skills and cushion.

steps.text: Start a small AI setup business with my friend Segun
Help Dad prepare his firm for robot trucks
Hold onto my savings and avoid silly spending
Build projects with AI tools on real systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, five years is perfect, enough time to be ready but short enough to stay sharp. I'd say people should build things now and not wait for the rules. I'd say it online, and probably at church, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about it. I'd graduate in 2029, and I'd have a company or a job and some savings by 2031. I'd have the right skills when AGI arrives, and a few years before the hands-on robots come in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and build a small business on the side, probably the AI setup service. I'd invest more of what I earn, and I'd help my dad plan the firm's future, maybe with robot-ready trucks. And I'd stay close to church friends, because people there help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and focused. It's a challenge, and I like challenges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would robot-ready trucks mean for your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope Dad could keep him on as a supervisor or a fleet checker. If not, I'd help find him a place, because family comes first. It's not a perfect answer, but I can't promise more than I can deliver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your faith fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It keeps me grounded. My pastor says to work hard, be generous and not be afraid, and I think that's good advice for any change. I'd tithe a bit more if I had a good year, and I'd want to give back.

say: I'd say five years is **perfect**, enough to be ready and short enough to stay sharp.
I'd tell people to **build things now** and not wait for the rules.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with a **company or job** and savings by 2031.
I'd have a few years before **hands-on robots** in 2034.
do: Finish the degree and run the **AI setup service** on the side.
Invest **more** of what I earn and help Dad plan the firm's future.
feel: I feel **calm and focused**, because I like challenges.
S3.quote: My pastor says to work hard, be generous and not be afraid, and I think that's good advice for any change
fieldNote: His **faith** and free-market views fit together: work hard, give back and don't fear.
Time makes the **plan** concrete: degree, side company, investing and a family business plan.
Family loyalty shows when he talks about his **uncle** and a place for him.

steps.text: Run an AI setup service for small firms on the side
Invest more of my earnings in index funds
Help Dad plan the firm's move to robot-ready trucks
Find a supervisor role for my uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, perfect, loads of time to build something real. I'd say anyone who wants to can learn, start and own something before it arrives. I'd say it's the best version, because it rewards work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel very good. A decade is a degree, a master's or a few years of work, and a proper business. I could be running a company with employees before the hands-on robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do a master's in something like machine learning, and build the business. I'd save and invest, get married and maybe buy a house. I'd also stay close to my parents and help the family firm grow into the new world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It's the one I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get married. Is there someone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a girl at church, Ada, who I like. It's early and she's doing nursing at another university, so we see each other on Sundays. I'd say with ten years I'd want to be settled by twenty-six or twenty-seven, with a business and a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make ten years go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I get arrogant, or get too comfortable because things are going well. I know that I'm lucky, because my parents can pay for me and I'm good with technology. I'd have to keep working and keep looking after the people around me.

say: I'd say **loads of time** to build something real, and it rewards work.
I'd say anyone who wants to can **learn, start and own** something.
think: A decade is a degree, a master's and a **proper business** with employees.
I'd be running a company before **hands-on robots** in 2039.
do: Finish the degree and do a **master's** in machine learning.
Save, invest, marry and **buy a house** while building the business.
feel: I feel **calm and excited**, since this is the one I'd choose.
S4.quote: I know that I'm lucky, because my parents can pay for me and I'm good with technology
fieldNote: Ten years gives him a **full life plan**: business, marriage, a house and help for the family firm.
He names his own **luck** unprompted, which tempers the free-market confidence.
His one fear is **arrogance**, which shows self-awareness.

steps.text: Do a master's in machine learning after the degree
Grow the AI setup business into a company with staff
Save and invest toward a house deposit
Help my parents grow the family logistics firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because it could undercut my dad's firm before it's ready, and his eleven drivers depend on him. What would help is time, a government that doesn't panic, and companies that keep loyal people on while they retrain them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm cold about this because I'm positive. I'm not cold, I just think the answer is to build and to look after your own people. I'd like to prove both can be done.

headlineQuote: I'm not cold, I just think the answer is to build and to look after your own people
portrait: Femi is a 19-year-old **physics** student from Manchester who uses AI all day and builds tools for his dad's trucks.
He is traditional in outlook: **faith, work, family** and free markets, with loyalty to his father's drivers.
Adaptive, he moves first: a **delivery app**, an index fund and plans for an AI setup business.
His mood stays calm or uneasy, never worse, because he trusts his skills and his family's **cushion**.
His main worry is his father's firm and its eleven **drivers** if robot trucks arrive early.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because it could undercut his dad's firm and its eleven drivers.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **time**, a government that doesn't panic and companies that keep loyal people on while they retrain them.
